summary: Ethan Sherbondy took a two-day Wilderness First Aid course at Boston College to prepare for the ride, and shared first-aid takeaways such as not giving aspirin for a suspected stroke and cooling heat stroke without causing shivering. He also signed up to teach an intro L-systems plant-modeling class for MIT Spark.
planning_notes: Two-day Wilderness First Aid course (SOLO field guide) was held at Boston College, a possible pre-trip training option for future riders.
First-aid reminders from the course: do not give aspirin for a suspected stroke; designate one leader in an emergency; cool heat-stroke patients but avoid shivering, which raises body temperature.

summary: Claire wrote about student-driven school design after MIT's digital learning director Sanjay Sarma spoke in a class, and about The Independent Project, a high school where students built their own school model.
planning_notes: The Independent Project (theindependentproject.org): a student-driven high school model the team cited as inspiration for its learning philosophy.

summary: The author taught an engineering class at MIT Spark to five 6th and 7th graders using the Helios kit the team planned to build on the trip, and reported what went wrong in prep: late-arriving parts, a part-fit failure, and borrowing tools at the last minute.
learning_festival: Not a Spokes Learning Festival: a test run of the Helios hardware class at MIT Spark (ESP) with five 6th-7th graders, supported by TAs Roger and Netia.
contacts: Dr. Kolitz (Draper Labs; funded the Spark class)
Danny Braunstein (MIT; donated $70 of servo motors)
MIT Hobby Shop (lent a table clamp)
Two MIT employees (lent box cutters)
Roger and Netia (TAs, MIT Spark)
planning_notes: Order parts at least three weeks ahead, especially servo motors from Hobbyking: very cheap but slow, and customer service is weak.
Fit-test every component before drilling or cutting; published dimensions were not enough, and six hours of prep were wasted when shafts did not fit the holes.
Critical components go out of stock and designs need last-minute changes (pulleys were unavailable), so build slack into the schedule.
Keep spare box cutters, clamps and small parts on hand; the team had to borrow them at the last minute.

summary: At TEDx Youth Charles River 2013 in MIT's Stata Center, speaker Romi Kadri introduced the team to Free Flow Bikes (UK), which agreed to donate bikes for the summer trip. The post also summarizes the other speakers' talks.
contacts: Romi Kadri (introduced the team to Free Flow Bikes at TEDx Youth Charles River 2013)
Free Flow Bikes (UK; donated bikes for the trip)
planning_notes: Free Flow Bikes (UK) donated the team's bikes after an introduction by Romi Kadri at TEDx Youth Charles River 2013 (MIT Stata Center, April 7, 2013).

summary: The post explains Carol Dweck's growth-mindset idea and says the summer's hands-on workshops are built to show children they can learn anything by doing.
planning_notes: Summer workshop design: hands-on projects (from growing vegetables to building solar panels) used to build a growth mindset in kids.

summary: An interview with Stefania Druga of Hackidemia on running open, hands-on kids' workshops, covering parent involvement, volunteer training and open space, and the team's questions about applying these ideas on the trip.
contacts: Stefania Druga (founder of Hackidemia; interviewed for this post)
planning_notes: Train local volunteers thoroughly so they can run follow-up classes after the team leaves; a single visit does not produce lasting learning.
Involve parents: kids take what they made home, and a parent who sees an activity is more likely to buy related toys.
Do not impose a fixed schedule per activity; let kids move freely between stations and keep the space open so they can see what others are building.
Idea to test: stay in a town for several days rather than one afternoon to build word-of-mouth turnout.
Hackidemia's mentor approach: keep things simple for kids and harder for mentors, who juggle new and advanced students.

summary: Turner, Ethan and Titiaan rode day one from San Francisco's Mojo Bicycle Cafe across the Golden Gate Bridge and up Conzelman Road (about 1,000 ft), where the team sketched a natural-phenomena book idea.
contacts: John O'Neil (board member, The Noyce Foundation; meeting planned in Sausalito, CA)
planning_notes: Day one out of San Francisco includes a roughly 1,000-ft climb up Conzelman Road for the Marin views; plan for it on the first day.

summary: A short pre-departure post on final errands, praising Mojo Bicycle Cafe in San Francisco as a coffee shop with a bike shop in the back.
planning_notes: Mojo Bicycle Cafe (San Francisco) combines coffee with a bike shop in the back; it was the team's start point and a useful pre-trip supply stop.

summary: The team held its launch party for friends and family at Crissy Field in San Francisco, and announced the next stops: an Oakland class, a ferry to Vallejo to start riding, and a Sacramento Learning Festival on Thursday.
learning_festival: Upcoming, no details given: an Oakland class the next day, then Learning Festival #3 in Sacramento on Thursday.

summary: The team ran its first two Learning Festivals in Oakland (Skyline High and Edna Brewer Middle), took the ferry from San Francisco to Vallejo to start riding, and camped at Lake Solano on night one while the van crew set up.
slept_at: Lake Solano campground, CA (camping night 1; van crew set up camp)
learning_festival: Oakland, CA. Day 1 at Skyline High in Michelle Shankar's chemistry room (four one-hour periods): EyeWire brain-mapping game (Claire), procedurally generated plants (Ethan), The Science of Music (Jeff), mousetrap car (Kaitlyn). Day 2 at Edna Brewer Middle School with 12-13 year olds: four classes taught twice, plus Titiaan's grow-your-own-plants-in-a-bottle class. Students started a gardening club.
contacts: Michelle Shankar (chemistry teacher, Skyline High, Oakland; hosted LF #1 and gave teaching feedback)
Joshua Guiterrez and Melissa Moritz (Teach for America, Oakland; introduced the school)
Edna Brewer Middle School, Oakland (hosted LF #2)
planning_notes: Expect to change lesson programs on the fly: LF #2 used a different program with younger kids (12-13) than the 14-18 target audience, and it worked.
The ferry from San Francisco to Vallejo was used as the first leg of the ride, with the van and the rest of the team going separately.
Davis, CA: Cloud Top Espresso and Juice was used as a mid-ride break stop.

summary: After a Learning Festival at PS7 middle school in Sacramento, the team rode into the Sierra foothills and camped outside Placerville, CA, while managing a tight food budget and noting that the kids wanted the program to continue.
slept_at: Campground just outside Placerville, CA (name not given); the night before was at a KOA in Sacramento
learning_festival: PS7 middle school in Sacramento on the last day of school (shares a campus with Sac High), 10 miles from the KOA. Claire taught EyeWire, Titiaan taught growing sprouts in a cup, Kaitlyn taught the mousetrap car. Students asked to come back and stay in touch, which prompted plans for a mentorship program.
contacts: PS7 middle school, Sacramento, CA (Learning Festival host)
planning_notes: The first hill day out of Sacramento left the team very hungry; oatmeal, sandwiches, pasta and eggs were the budget staples.
Internet access was expected to be unreliable for the days after Placerville, CA; plan offline navigation and messaging.

summary: Ten days in, the team had crossed California and Nevada, and the post highlights 5 a.m. starts, free ice cream from new friends, and showers in public park sprinklers.
planning_notes: Public park sprinklers were used as showers in California and Nevada.

summary: Over one week the team crossed Nevada on US-50 ('Loneliest Road in America'), received trail magic in Genoa, Middlegate and Ely, and ended the week with a host for the night in Ely.
slept_at: Thomas and Jen's home, Ely, NV (offered after the team met Thomas at Economy Drugs)
contacts: Thomas and Jen (hosts, Ely, NV; Thomas met the team at Economy Drugs)
Hosts at Middlegate, NV (name not given; hosted the team for burgers and internet)
Woman in a Genoa, NV deli (name not given; bought the team ice cream)
planning_notes: US-50 in Nevada ('Loneliest Road in America'): over 300 miles from the state line with very few services; plan food and water for long gaps.
Middlegate, NV (population 17) has fast internet and giant burgers; a welcome stop on US-50.
Economy Drugs in Ely, NV sells espresso and general store items; Ely (about 4,000 people) was the biggest town in several days.
Nevada headwinds were hard after the Sierras; budget extra time for wind on the desert stretch.

summary: The team stopped on the road to talk with Jonah, a 19-year-old walking east to west across the country and trying to complete the walking 'grand slam' of four long trails.
contacts: Jonah (19-year-old walker; location not stated, heading through Nevada and California)

summary: The team placed the order for official Spokes apparel, funded by edX, 16 days into the trip.
contacts: edX (funded the team apparel)
planning_notes: edX funded the official team apparel order, placed 16 days into the trip.

summary: The post is only a title and photo: the team crossed into a new state and timezone, which is Utah given the route (see the same-day Cedar City post).
At Cedar City, UT, a couple of team members stopped at Starbucks for Ethan's birthday mocha, and a local woman, Nancy, gave the team a gift card for future stops.
contacts: Nancy (Cedar City, UT; bought the team a Starbucks gift card)
planning_notes: Starbucks in Cedar City, UT is a coffee stop on the route; Nancy's gift card was redeemed at a Starbucks in Montrose, CO on July 5.

summary: The team rode through Capitol Reef National Park in 107-degree heat after a 2,800-ft climb to start the day, and reached 1,000 total miles.
planning_notes: Capitol Reef National Park (Utah): a 2,800-ft climb to start the day, then a scenic downhill through the park; at 107 degrees, start early.

summary: Nathan released a video of the California leg of the trip, and the team moved on to Colorado.
planning_notes: Nathan rode with pounds of camera equipment in his panniers to film the trip; plan pannier weight and space for a media rider.

summary: On a 108-degree day the team rode Hanksville to Hite, UT, sheltered in shade until a 2 a.m. night ride of about 80 miles to Blanding, UT. The post also notes Nathan's video is out and the team is about to cross into Colorado.
contacts: Pat and Dan (UConn Medical School riders doing Coast to Coast for a Cure 2013; met on the road in Utah)
planning_notes: Hite, UT (Colorado River recreation area): the convenience store closes at 3:30 p.m., and the next services are about 80 miles away toward Blanding; stock up on water and food before.
Hanksville to Hite is 50 miles of exposed desert with shade only at the base of the canyons.
Heat: 108 degrees before noon at Hite; night riding (starting at 2 a.m.) worked. Plan early or night starts for Utah desert stretches in summer.
The map-based climb profile was misleading: the final stretch before Blanding (miles 60-80) was the steepest climb yet. Check elevation profiles, not just mileage.
Pat and Dan offered the team use of their motel pool in Blanding, UT.

summary: The team rode Telluride to Montrose (a July 4 fireworks night ride), a 106-mile day to Sargent at the base of Monarch Pass (11,312 ft), a KOA, Fairplay, a night inside Bailey's Cutthroat Cafe, a Loveland library Learning Festival, a Boulder break day, and then reached Colorado Springs.
slept_at: Several nights: KOA after Monarch Pass, CO; Cutthroat Cafe in Bailey, CO (owner Chip let the team sleep inside)
learning_festival: Loveland, CO public library (the day after Bailey): each small group picked one class (3D printing, mechanical engineering, Jeff's psychology of music) for students ranging from 3rd grade to recent high school grads. A host family in Loveland put the team up.
contacts: Chip (owner, Cutthroat Cafe, Bailey, CO; offered sleep indoors and breakfast)
Java Moose cafe staff (Fairplay, CO; a barista took Jeff to an EMT for vitals)
Starbucks in Montrose, CO (gave the team half off drinks after hearing about Spokes)
Loveland, CO host family (name not given)
planning_notes: Monarch Pass (11,312 ft, Continental Divide, the highest point on the route) is followed by about 30 mostly downhill miles.
KOA after the pass: gorgeous, has horses, and complimentary coffee (the team drank a lot of it); a campground option near the pass.
Altitude: an EMT check in Fairplay showed Ethan's oxygen saturation was low while Jeff's was high. Take altitude symptoms seriously after Monarch Pass.
Fairplay, CO: Java Moose cafe has wifi, excellent espresso and chai almonds, a good stop before the Bailey stretch.

About 40 miles from Fairplay to Bailey, the team had no pre-booked camping because they had left the Adventure Cycling route to attend Spokes events; plan hosts or campsites in advance for off-route stretches.
A derailleur worked loose on hills near Bailey and fell into the chain; with no proper tool or expertise, the team had to hitchhike for help. Carry the right tool and know the nearest bike shop.
Cutthroat Cafe in Bailey, CO: owner offered the team indoor sleeping and breakfast; cafe hosting is a useful lodging option.
Montrose to Sargent (July 5) was 106 miles, including a 6-mile detour for the Montrose Starbucks.

summary: After a northern Colorado detour that added a couple hundred miles, the team rode from Colorado Springs toward Pueblo, took 22 miles of gravel road onto the Transamerica trail, and welcomed Noor Razzak as the ninth team member to document the trip.
slept_at: Host family in Colorado Springs, CO (Jade, Eva and Dillon)
contacts: Host family in Colorado Springs, CO (Jade, Eva and Dillon; hosted the team before Pueblo)
planning_notes: Gravel road of about 22 miles on the way toward Pueblo, CO, where the Western Express trail meets the Transamerica trail: Titiaan's Santos handled it well, while the Jamis touring bikes struggled.
Pueblo, CO: the team missed the downtown and with it the last real coffee shop for a long stretch; plan a coffee stop in Pueblo itself.
Gas stations near Pueblo, CO had wifi, useful where cell coverage is poor.
Flat terrain east of Colorado Springs: the team averaged about 22 mph over the first 31 miles of the planned 95-mile day.

summary: A reflective post inspired by Roberto Carlos Rivera's talk at the Unreasonable Institute, arguing that adversity builds character and that shielding children from it may leave them hopeless.
The team enjoyed the flat, scenic Kansas riding, visited the Cosmosphere in Hutchinson, had a bike repaired in Newton, and planned to meet an MIT friend who would guest-ride to St. Louis.
contacts: Chase Lambert (MIT friend; planned to guest-cycle to St. Louis)
Bike shop in Newton, KS (name not given; repaired a severely bent derailleur)
planning_notes: Newton, KS: a shop repaired a severely bent derailleur and the bike rode smoothly afterward.
Kansas heat: the team rode in the evening to avoid the worst of the day's heat.
Cosmosphere museum in Hutchinson, KS (aviation and space exhibits) was a good sightseeing stop.
All-you-can-eat buffets were used as cheap meals on the route in Kansas.
Kansas City was the next planned teaching stop.

summary: At a 24-hour Learning Festival on a Millstadt, Illinois farm, 30 St. Louis homeschool teens brainstormed projects, and one team designed and fired a trebuchet in about five hours. The post reflects on why projects succeeded and where they stalled.
learning_festival: 24-hour Learning Festival on Carrie's farm in Millstadt, IL with 30 teens from the St. Louis Homeschool Network: three hours of engineering classes, then a brainstorm where eight students pitched ideas. The trebuchet team, a video game and an automated waffle-maker alarm clock each finished something; three teams lost interest the next morning.
contacts: Carrie (farm host, Millstadt, IL; provided beams, drills, a saw and a metal rod)
St. Louis Homeschool Network (partner group for the Learning Festival)
planning_notes: Schedule at least three hours after the brainstorm so every team can take a first physical step; the old format (a list of actions with no building) lost momentum.
Keep prototyping materials close to the workshop; the Millstadt farm had beams, two drills, a saw and a metal rod on site.
Specific project ideas ('improve your school') got finished; vague ideas stalled.
Open question: how to keep the project model going year-round, including a project kit students can use without a mentor.
